research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. What `java.security.KeyPair` governs, and what the finding refers to

`java.security.KeyPair` is a **final, serializable holder** for one `PublicKey` and one `PrivateKey`. Its documented API consists of the constructor `KeyPair(PublicKey, PrivateKey)` and the accessors `getPublic()` and `getPrivate()`. Oracle explicitly states that the class “does not enforce any security” and, once initialized, should be handled like a `PrivateKey`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

The reported wording is **not a documented JCA exception, return value, or API event**. In particular, neither Oracle’s `KeyPair` API nor its JCA guide defines a “KeyPairSpec” finding category or an `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls` condition. The only documented Java events directly corresponding to that wording are:

* construction: `new KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey)`, and
* retrieval of the stored components: `getPublic()` / `getPrivate()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

For this particular CrySL source, “no construction … was observed” can be tied only to the rule’s named constructor event `Con` and its event-order/provenance expressions—not to an Oracle-defined `KeyPair` runtime failure. The source alone does not identify the detector’s trace, call site, analysis revision/configuration, or the precise meaning of the reported error category. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

There is also an important API distinction: a new key pair can be produced by `KeyPairGenerator.generateKeyPair()` or `genKeyPair()`, whereas the CrySL file’s `Con` event is spelled as the `KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey)` constructor. The JCA API documents the generator methods as generating a key pair; the rule text does not list either generator method as an event. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))

### 2. Documented correct/safe usage and official remediation

**Documented `KeyPair` usage**

* Construct it from a `PublicKey` and a `PrivateKey`.
* Obtain references to those same components via `getPublic()` and `getPrivate()`.
* The constructor stores component references rather than copying them; Oracle documents that as safe because `Key` objects are immutable.
* Treat an initialized `KeyPair` as sensitive like a `PrivateKey`, because the holder itself provides no security enforcement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

**Related documented JCA facilities**

* For creating a fresh asymmetric pair, `KeyPairGenerator` is the JCA class documented for generating public/private key pairs. Oracle recommends explicitly initializing the generator rather than depending on provider defaults, because provider defaults may differ and can change in a future version. This is a recommendation about `KeyPairGenerator`, not a `KeyPair` constructor requirement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPairGenerator.html))
* For reconstructing key objects from key material/specifications, `KeyFactory` is documented as converting between `Key` objects and `KeySpec` representations; it supplies `generatePublic(KeySpec)` and `generatePrivate(KeySpec)`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyFactory.html))

**Official remediation status**

Oracle’s `KeyPair` documentation does **not** define an invalid method-call sequence and does **not** prescribe a remediation for use “otherwise.” It therefore provides no official fix for the reported CrySL finding specifically. The applicable source-supported guidance is limited to the APIs above: construct a holder from component keys, generate a new pair through `KeyPairGenerator` where generation is required, or use `KeyFactory` for supported key-spec conversions. Which of those semantics applies cannot be determined from the finding text alone. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

### 3. Compatibility, persisted/wire formats, version support, and migration

**Platform/API availability**

* `KeyPair` is documented as available since Java 1.1. Its constructor and two accessors are the longstanding core API. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))
* In the current Java SE 26 API, `KeyPair` additionally implements `DEREncodable` as a **preview** API. `DEREncodable` is documented since Java 25, requires preview features to be enabled, and may be removed or made permanent in a future release. Code that relies on this newer interface has a different platform requirement from code using the longstanding constructor/accessors. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))

**Persisted form**

`KeyPair` implements `Serializable`. Java SE 26’s serialized-form documentation declares serialVersionUID `-7565189502268009837L` and records two serialized fields: `privateKey` and `publicKey`. Java SE 17 documents the same serialVersionUID and fields. That is evidence of an unchanged declared serialized form across those two documented releases, but it is **not** a general guarantee that every concrete key implementation or provider can deserialize across every environment. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/serialized-form.html))

Oracle separately cautions that serialized `Key` material may be sensitive and should not be exposed in untrusted environments. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

**Wire/interchange format**

`KeyPair` itself does not document a standalone wire format in its class API. The associated `Key` interface instead describes **component-key** encodings: keys may have standard external encodings, such as X.509 `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` for public keys and PKCS#8 for private keys; a key may also return `null` if it does not support encoding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))

Oracle’s JCA guide describes `X509EncodedKeySpec` as the DER encoding of a public key and `PKCS8EncodedKeySpec` as the DER encoding of a private key. It also says `KeyFactory` can convert between `Key` and compatible `KeySpec` representations where that operation is possible; hardware-held keys may not be convertible. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/security/security-developer-guide.pdf))

**Migration path**

No official `KeyPair` migration path is documented for changing from direct construction to generator- or factory-originated component keys. There is likewise no documented assertion that such a change preserves a specific serialized object stream, component encoding, provider behavior, or external protocol. Compatibility therefore remains unresolved without the concrete key algorithms, providers, storage format, and platform versions.

### 4. Exact applicability of `KeyPair.crysl`

Primary rule source:  
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl

The rule identifies the governed API with the following clause:

```text
SPEC java.security.KeyPair
```

Its declared event variables identify constructor inputs and accessor results as `java.security.PublicKey` / `java.security.PrivateKey`. The matching event clauses are:

```text
c1: KeyPair(publicKey, privateKey);
gpu1: retPublicKey = getPublic();
gpr1: retPrivateKey = getPrivate();
```

The rule therefore names:

| Event alias | Named API member | Parameter-list constraint stated by the rule |
|---|---|---|
| `Con` / `c1` | `KeyPair` constructor | Two arguments: `publicKey` and `privateKey`, declared in the rule as `java.security.PublicKey` and `java.security.PrivateKey` |
| `GetPubl` / `gpu1` | `getPublic` | Empty parameter list: `getPublic()` |
| `GetPriv` / `gpr1` | `getPrivate` | Empty parameter list: `getPrivate()` |

The source’s event order is:

```text
Con, (GetPubl | GetPriv)*
```

The source then evaluates these requirements, including the condition specifically relevant when no `Con` call occurs:

```text
generatedPrivkey[privateKey];
generatedPubkey[publicKey];
noCallTo[Con] => generatedKeypair[this, _];
```

It ensures the pair/key predicates after the respective events:

```text
generatedKeypair[this, _] after Con;
generatedPubkey[retPublicKey] after GetPubl;
generatedPrivkey[retPrivateKey] after GetPriv;
```

All quoted clauses are from the supplied primary rule source. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

**Can it match a method merely because it shares a name?** **No, not as the rule is stated.** The rule is scoped by the explicit declaration `SPEC java.security.KeyPair`; it is not written as a global, name-only matcher for every `getPublic`, `getPrivate`, or `KeyPair`-named method/constructor. The file itself does not document the analyzer’s type-resolution or dispatch implementation, however, so the exact mechanics by which a particular analyzer enforces that scope are not established by this source alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))

## Source limitations and unresolved questions

* The CrySL file states a protocol, predicate requirements, and predicate effects. It does **not** define the detector label `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls`, explain “KeyPairSpec,” or provide a finding trace. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/KeyPair.crysl))
* Oracle’s `KeyPair` API documents a holder object; it does not document a verification that the constructor inputs are mathematically corresponding public/private components. It also says the class does not itself enforce security. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/KeyPair.html))
* Persisted/wire-format compatibility cannot be concluded from `KeyPair` alone because concrete key implementations, providers, algorithms, and whether encoding is supported affect the result. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Key.html))
